terms.comment: Traupman writes octō, the regular form. Lewis & Short prints octŏ with a short final vowel, a shortened form.

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, cited by printed page; each phrase checked against the searchable text of the book.
Lewis & Short: octo

octo-long.html: The inherited form, with the long vowel of Greek ὀκτώ; Allen & Greenough’s table of numerals (§133) and Traupman (253) print octō. Lewis & Short’s octŏ is a shortened form.
